description: Orderable pages with rich-text content, plus a Settings singleton for the site title.

pages.title: Getting started
pages.body:
Relay forwards webhooks from the services you use to the endpoints you control, and keeps a record of every delivery. This page gets you from nothing to a delivered event in about five minutes.

## Install the CLI

```bash
npm install -g @relay/cli
relay login
```

`relay login` opens a browser once and stores a token in `~/.relay/config.json`. Everything after this works offline until the token expires.

## Create your first endpoint

An endpoint is a URL Relay delivers to, plus the events it should receive.

```bash
relay endpoints create \
  --url https://api.example.com/hooks/stripe \
  --events payment.succeeded,payment.failed
```

Relay answers with an endpoint id and a signing secret. Store the secret the way you store database passwords — you need it to verify that a request really came from Relay.

## Send a test event

```bash
relay send payment.succeeded --data '{"amount": 4200}'
```

Watch it arrive with `relay tail`. If the endpoint returns anything other than a 2xx, Relay retries on the schedule described in [Retries and delivery](retries.html).

pages.title: Authentication
pages.body:
Every request to the Relay API carries an API key in the `Authorization` header. Keys belong to a project, never to a person, so removing a teammate never breaks a running integration.

## Using a key

```bash
curl https://api.relay.dev/v1/endpoints \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer rl_live_8f3a…"
```

Keys are prefixed so you can tell at a glance what you are holding: `rl_live_` for production, `rl_test_` for the sandbox. Test keys accept the same calls but never deliver to real endpoints.

## Rotating a key

Create the new key first, deploy it, then delete the old one:

```bash
relay keys create --name "api-2026-08"
relay keys delete rl_live_8f3a…
```

Deletion takes effect immediately and cannot be undone. A deleted key returns `401 invalid_key`, which your client should treat as fatal rather than retrying.

## Verifying deliveries

Relay signs every delivery with the endpoint's secret. Compute the HMAC over the raw request body — not the parsed JSON — and compare it in constant time:

```js
const expected = crypto
  .createHmac('sha256', secret)
  .update(rawBody)
  .digest('hex')
```

pages.title: Sending events
pages.body:
An event is a name and a JSON payload. Relay does not inspect the payload beyond its size, so the shape is yours to define.

```bash
curl https://api.relay.dev/v1/events \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $RELAY_KEY" \
  -d '{"name":"order.shipped","data":{"order":"A-1183"}}'
```

## Naming events

Use `noun.verb`, past tense, lowercase: `order.shipped`, `invoice.paid`, `user.deleted`. Subscribers can then match on a prefix (`order.*`) instead of enumerating every name you might add later.

## Payload limits

- 256 KB per event body
- 40 events per second per project, bursting to 200
- 30 days of history on the free plan, 12 months on paid

Anything larger than 256 KB should be a reference — an object key, a row id — that the receiver fetches. Webhooks are notifications, not a transport for files.

## Idempotency

Include an `idempotency_key` and Relay drops duplicates for 24 hours. Retries of your own request are then free of consequences, which matters when a timeout leaves you unsure whether the first call landed.

pages.title: Retries and delivery
pages.body:
A delivery attempt succeeds when your endpoint answers `2xx` within 10 seconds. Everything else is a failure, and Relay retries.

## The schedule

Attempts back off: immediately, then after 30 seconds, 5 minutes, 30 minutes, 2 hours, 6 hours, and finally 24 hours. After the last attempt the event is marked `undelivered` and stays available for replay.

## Replaying

```bash
relay replay --endpoint ep_2f8c --since 2026-08-01
```

Replay sends the original payload with a new signature and a new `attempt` number. Receivers that respect `idempotency_key` can replay a month of history without side effects.

## Circuit breaking

Twenty consecutive failures pause an endpoint and email the project owners. Nothing is lost — paused endpoints keep queueing — but Relay stops hammering a service that is clearly down. Resume with `relay endpoints resume ep_2f8c`.

## Ordering

Relay does not guarantee order. Two events emitted a millisecond apart can arrive in either sequence, and a retry can land after a newer event. Include a timestamp or a version in your payload and ignore anything older than what you have already processed.

pages.title: The CLI
pages.body:
The CLI is a thin wrapper over the same API the dashboard uses. Anything you can click, you can script.

## Tailing traffic

```bash
relay tail --endpoint ep_2f8c --status failed
```

Output is one line per attempt: timestamp, event name, response status, duration. Add `--json` to pipe it into `jq`.

## Local development

`relay forward` receives events on your machine without a public URL:

```bash
relay forward --to http://localhost:3000/hooks
```

The tunnel closes with the process. Events that arrive while it is down are queued and delivered when you reconnect, so you can stop and start the server freely.

## Configuration as files

`relay pull` writes your endpoints to `relay.json`; `relay push` applies changes. Commit the file and your webhook configuration lives in review alongside the code that depends on it.

pages.title: Rate limits
pages.body:
Limits are per project and reset on a rolling window. The response headers tell you where you stand:

```
X-RateLimit-Limit: 40
X-RateLimit-Remaining: 12
X-RateLimit-Reset: 1786012800
```

## When you exceed them

The API returns `429 rate_limited` with a `Retry-After` header in seconds. Respect it; retrying sooner extends the window. The CLI already does this for you.

## Raising a limit

Paid projects start at 200 events per second. Beyond that, write to support with a rough shape of your traffic — steady rate, expected burst, and the endpoints involved. Limits are raised per project, not per key.

pages.title: Errors
pages.body:
Errors are JSON, with a stable `code` you can branch on and a `message` written for a human reading a log.

```json
{
  "error": {
    "code": "endpoint_not_found",
    "message": "No endpoint with id ep_9xk1 in this project."
  }
}
```

## Codes worth handling

- `invalid_key` — the key was deleted or belongs to another project. Fatal; do not retry.
- `rate_limited` — back off for `Retry-After` seconds.
- `payload_too_large` — the body exceeded 256 KB. Send a reference instead.
- `endpoint_paused` — the circuit breaker tripped. The event is queued, not lost.

## What we never do

We never return a `2xx` for a failed operation, and we never change an error's `code` once it has shipped. Messages get clearer over time; codes are a contract.

settings.title: Relay docs
settings.tagline: A webhook relay you can reason about
settings.intro:
Relay forwards webhooks from the services you use to the endpoints you control, retries what fails, and keeps every attempt on record so you can replay it later.

Start with [Getting started](getting-started.html) for a delivered event in five minutes, or jump to [Authentication](authentication.html) if you are wiring up a production key.
